title: Edgewater CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Near Edgewater, median well depth is 28 ft and median yield is 10.2 gpm. Learn about drilling costs, water levels and contamination risks.
h1: Water wells and drilling around Edgewater, Colorado
intro_html:
Around Edgewater, wells are much shallower than most people expect for the Front Range, but they sit in the Denver Basin system and urban geology brings its own issues. The Colorado DWR has records for 11,506 wells within about 5 miles, with 6,308 listing a total depth.

If you are buying a place in Edgewater, Lakewood, Wheat Ridge or nearby, you should be looking at depth, yield and water quality, not just whether there is a permit on file. Here is what the local records actually show.

sections.heading: How deep wells run around Edgewater
sections.html:
Within about 5 miles of Edgewater, the median well depth is only 28 feet, and the middle half of wells fall between 20 and 47 feet. That is very shallow by Colorado standards. About 88% of reported wells are under 100 feet deep, and only 2% go beyond 600 feet, with the deepest at 1,997 feet.

This tells you two things. First, many older and monitoring wells are just tapping shallow alluvium or weathered bedrock. Second, when a domestic or commercial well has to chase deeper Denver Basin zones, the depth can jump fast. When you get a drilling bid, make sure the footage allowance covers at least into the 100–300 foot range, even though many neighbors are shallower.

sections.heading: Water table depth and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water levels here are generally shallow. The median depth to water is 14 feet, with the middle half between 10 and 19 feet below ground. That is consistent with alluvial and shallow bedrock conditions along this urban stretch between Lakeside, Mountain View and Lakewood.

The decade-by-decade medians bounce between 13 and 16 feet (13 in the 1950s, 16 in the 1960s, 13 in the 2000s, 16 in the 2010s, 13 in the 2020s). That pattern does not suggest a steady decline, more a flat trend with normal ups and downs. Still, shallow water also means you must pay attention to surface contamination and proper sealing, not just how far the driller has to go.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Of the 290 wells that report a pump test, the median yield is 10.2 gpm, with the middle half between 8.0 and 15.0 gpm. About 61% of wells fall in the 5–15 gpm range and 29% report more than 15 gpm, which is plenty for a typical household and some outdoor use.

On the downside, 3% of wells come in under 1 gpm and another 8% produce only 1–5 gpm. So roughly one in nine tested wells is marginal for heavier use without storage. In fractured bedrock and Denver Basin settings, yields can vary a lot over short distances. Before you buy a lot, compare several nearby well permits and pay attention to both depth and reported gpm.

sections.heading: Who is drilling here and when wells went in
sections.html:
Drilling around Edgewater and nearby Wheat Ridge and Berkley has been steady for decades. Permit counts climbed from 266 in the 1950s to 480 in the 1970s, then jumped to 2,199 in the 1990s and 2,406 in the 2000s. There are still plenty of new wells going in, with 1,619 permits in the 2010s and 825 already in the 2020s, up through the newest permits in 2025.

Most activity is in the Denver Basin aquifers, with 100% of the specified aquifer wells tied into that system. The most active drillers in the records include Authorized (Pe, Pg), Adams Water Well Drilling (Adams, George E), and Ground Exploration Llc (Bender, Joseph T.). When you talk to a driller, ask for permits they have completed in Edgewater and Lakewood specifically, not just elsewhere on the Front Range.

sections.heading: Typical cost for a new well near Edgewater
sections.html:
The drilling here is mainly Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, which tends to run in a predictable $50–$70 per foot range. At the local median depth of 28 feet, the bare drilled hole pencils out to roughly $1,400–$2,000. By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical, you are generally looking at about $7,400–$14,000 for a finished domestic well.

If your driller thinks you may need to go closer to the 90th percentile depth of 109 feet, scale those numbers up accordingly. A deeper Denver Basin completion, or chasing water toward several hundred feet or more, can move the total into a much higher bracket, so make sure the contract spells out per-foot pricing beyond the base depth.

sections.heading: Environmental and water-quality risks around Edgewater
sections.html:
Unlike a remote ranch area, this part of Jefferson County sits in a heavily studied and impacted urban corridor. Within about 10 miles, there are 649 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 97 historic mine features, and 183 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. It is no accident that 55% of the local well permits are for monitoring, not just supply; domestic and household use is about 25%, and irrigation around 3%.

Shallow alluvial and bedrock wells, with typical water levels around 10–19 feet down, are more vulnerable to surface and legacy contamination. If you are buying a home or lot, budget for a full lab panel on an existing well and consider ongoing testing, especially if you are anywhere near known industrial areas between Edgewater and East Pleasant View.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well lot near Edgewater
sections.html:
For an existing home, pull the DWR well permit, check the reported depth, yield and static level, and then compare those to several neighboring wells in Edgewater, Wheat Ridge and Lakewood. A 20–50 foot well with around 8–15 gpm and a water level at 10–20 feet is common here, but you still want a recent water-quality test given the number of contamination and monitoring sites in the area.

On vacant land, assume you will need a Denver Basin domestic permit and design around the 35 gpm exempt pumping limit. Coordinate well and septic locations so setbacks work on the actual surveyed lot. Get a written drilling proposal that covers deeper footage scenarios and make closing contingent on successfully completing and testing a well, not just on obtaining a permit.

faq.q: How deep are water wells around Edgewater, Colorado?
faq.a: Well records within about 5 miles of Edgewater show a median depth of 28 feet, with the middle half between 20 and 47 feet. About 88% of reported wells are under 100 feet deep, and the 90th percentile is 109 feet. A small fraction reach much deeper Denver Basin targets, including a deepest recorded well at 1,997 feet.

faq.q: How much water do wells near Edgewater usually produce?
faq.a: For the 290 wells that list a pump test, the median yield is 10.2 gpm and the middle half fall between 8.0 and 15.0 gpm. Around 61% of wells sit in the 5–15 gpm band and 29% exceed 15 gpm. On the low side, 3% are under 1 gpm and 8% are between 1 and 5 gpm, which can be limiting without storage.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well near Edgewater, CO?
faq.a: In the Denver Basin bedrock around Edgewater, typical drilling rates run about $50–$70 per foot. At the local median depth of 28 feet, that is roughly $1,400–$2,000 for the hole. A complete domestic well with casing, pump, tank, trenching and electrical usually lands in the $7,400–$14,000 range, with deeper wells costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in the Edgewater area?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. The area has 649 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 183 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, and 55% of local wells are for monitoring. With shallow water levels around 10–19 feet, you should always test an existing well for a full lab panel before relying on it for drinking water.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels dropping near Edgewater, Colorado?
faq.a: The static water level data here do not show a clear long-term decline. Median depths to water were 13 feet in the 1950s, 16 feet in the 1960s, 13 feet in the 2000s, 16 feet in the 2010s, and 13 feet in the 2020s. Overall, that points to a relatively flat trend, though individual wells can behave differently due to local geology and pumping patterns.
